design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, random-order crossover laboratory study in 32 healthy volunteers (16 women, 16 men) at the University of Basel: one session with a single oral dose of MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) in gelatin capsules and one with identical placebo capsules (64 sessions), at least 10 days apart. The paper lists two ClinicalTrials.gov numbers (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685). Measures: visual analogue scales (happy, open, close to others) and the 60-item Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS) repeatedly; the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET, 120 trials) 3 hours after the dose; the Social Value Orientation (SVO) test, a paper money-allocation task, 4 hours after; a dynamic Face Emotion Recognition Task (FERT) 2 hours after; plasma oxytocin, copeptin, cortisol, prolactin and testosterone; plasma MDMA. Peak changes from baseline were analysed with analyses of variance (drug within person; sex between people), Tukey post hoc tests and correlations; session order and past cannabis use were tested as extra factors.
can_establish: Whether, in 32 healthy young adults (22 with no earlier MDMA use, 10 with fewer than five uses), a single oral dose of MDMA raised self-ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others and several mood scales (well-being, extroversion, activity, emotional excitation, dreaminess; also inactivity and introversion) against placebo; raised ratings of feeling for people shown in photographs (emotional empathy) across all volunteers; lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces but not happy faces; and raised plasma oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin, as measured in a hospital laboratory over the hours after the dose (the tasks at 2 to 4 hours).
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA changes how people treat others outside the laboratory (the tasks are photographs, a computer test and a paper allocation of sums whose size is not stated, with real payment to two volunteers); whether the effects on empathy and prosocial behaviour exist in women or only in men, or differ between the sexes at all (the sex-specific results are post hoc subgroup tests of 16 people each, among at least 42 uncorrected tests); whether results are free of expectancy (the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had); the size of any effect (the text prints test statistics, not means; means are in Figures 1 to 3 and Supplementary Table S1, not read); anything about other doses, repeated doses or MDMA taken in a social, party or therapy setting; whether oxytocin carries the effect (no correlation was found).

sample.recruitment: Recruited from the University of Basel campus and paid for taking part (Materials and Methods > Participants; Experimental protocol).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: a personal or first-degree relative history of psychiatric disorder; chronic or acute physical illness; smoking; a lifetime history of more than five uses of illicit drugs (past cannabis allowed); any illicit drug use including cannabis in the last 2 months or during the study (repeated urine tests at screening and before each session). Women were tested in the follicular phase (days 2 to 14) of the cycle (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.demographics: Mean age 25 (SD 3), range 20 to 31; 16 men and 16 women. 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier experiences; 19 had used cannabis more than five times and 15 other illicit drugs one to four times (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.attrition: None reported; every analysis is described for the 32. The inequality-aversion test has 20 error degrees of freedom and the plasma MDMA comparison between sexes 15, without saying which volunteers or how many were analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Young university volunteers, screened for health, mostly new to MDMA, tested in a hospital unit; people with psychiatric disorders, regular drug use or smoking are absent by design. Paid volunteers who agreed to take MDMA for research.

exposure.measurement: MDMA (Lipomed AG, Arlesheim, Switzerland) in gelatin capsules with mannitol filler, identical mannitol placebo; plasma MDMA measured repeatedly by high-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (Cmax 209 ng/mL in men and 269.9 in women, SEM 6.4 and 9.3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral dose of 125 mg in one session (1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30; 1.68 in men and 2.09 in women) and placebo in the other, at least 10 days apart; the tasks were run 2 hours (faces), 3 hours (empathy test) and 4 hours (money allocation) after the dose (Study drug; Experimental protocol; Measures).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use including cannabis excluded for 2 months before and during the study (urine tests at screening and before each session); smokers excluded; no information on alcohol.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 months free of illicit drugs by history, with repeated urine tests (TRIAGE 8) at screening and before each session.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the same people (double-blind, random order, washout at least 10 days); the sexes are compared with each other (16 against 16, different people).
comparison.matching: Within person for MDMA against placebo. The authors say order effects were excluded with session order as a factor and that past cannabis use did not confound the sex-by-drug interaction; no statistics are printed for either.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Trait empathy was measured once (Interpersonal Reactivity Index) and did not change the response to MDMA; mood and expectation before the sessions are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded by screening and urine tests.

outcomes.instruments: Visual analogue scales (happy, open, close to others); AMRS (60 items); Multifaceted Empathy Test (40 photographs of people in emotionally charged scenes, each tested for cognitive empathy as percent correct, explicit emotional empathy and implicit emotional empathy rated 1 to 9, 20 positive and 20 negative scenes); Social Value Orientation (six primary and nine secondary slider items; the angle of the mean amount allocated to the other person against self; allocated funds had real value for two randomly drawn volunteers); dynamic Face Emotion Recognition Task (accuracy and detection threshold per emotion); Interpersonal Reactivity Index (trait empathy); plasma oxytocin, copeptin, cortisol, prolactin, testosterone (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Tasks cited to earlier work (Dziobek 2008; Murphy 2011; Domes 2008); the dynamic FERT is described as novel; the paper cross-checked the MET against the FERT after placebo (r = 0.42).
outcomes.operationalization: Repeated measures as peak change from baseline; single-time-point tasks compared between drug sessions. The 60-item AMRS is reported only for the scales that changed, and for anxiety, which did not; the number of scales is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated; Tukey post hoc tests after significant analysis-of-variance effects. Editors' count of 42 tests with a printed statistic in the Results (3 visual analogue scales, 7 AMRS scales and 1 sex interaction, 6 empathy tests and 2 post hoc, 4 SVO tests, 16 face-recognition tests, 3 hormone tests); the supplement, not read, holds more. The authors name the number of comparisons as a limitation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind with identical capsules, but the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had during the session and that this may have biased task performance. Outcomes are self-ratings and tasks; no blinding check is reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: No means, SDs or effect sizes are printed in the text; the values are in the figures and Supplementary Table S1 (not read). Printed test statistics, F(1,31) unless stated: happy 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52, AMRS well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, emotional excitation 28.46, dreaminess 25.48, activity 24.48 (all p < 0.001), introversion 10.05 (p = 0.003), inactivity 7.72 (p = 0.009); anxiety scale not raised (no statistic). Emotional empathy, all volunteers: explicit 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047); positive scenes explicit 8.60 (p = 0.006) and implicit 5.02 (p = 0.032); negative scenes not significant; treatment-by-sex interaction implicit 4.68 (p = 0.039) and explicit 3.03 (p = 0.092); post hoc in men explicit p = 0.025 and implicit p = 0.022, in women not significant; cognitive empathy unchanged. SVO angle 4.42 (p = 0.044), by sex 5.52 (p = 0.026), post hoc men p = 0.008, women not significant; inequality-aversion F(1,20) 3.39 (p = 0.079). Face recognition accuracy overall 28.63 (p < 0.001), by sex 6.04 (p = 0.020), women p < 0.001, men not significant; fearful 14.90, angry 18.60 (p < 0.001), disgusted 5.81 (p = 0.022), surprised 9.79 (p = 0.004), happy 0.27 (p = 0.607); in women only fearful (p < 0.001), angry (p = 0.007) and sad (p = 0.010); fear detection threshold 4.92 (printed P < 0.032). Hormones: oxytocin 19.84, cortisol 98.70, prolactin 127.81 (p < 0.001); copeptin and testosterone not changed; no correlation of hormones with empathy or prosocial effects. Women's peak plasma MDMA 269.9 against men's 209 ng/mL (F(1,15) 35.73).
analysis.covariates: Drug within and sex between people; session order and past cannabis use as extra factors (stated, no statistics); trait empathy as a median split for the empathy test; no adjustment for dose per kilogram, although women received 2.09 and men 1.68 mg/kg.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper states the study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685). The registry records were not read, so whether the empathy, prosocial and face-recognition outcomes reported here match the registered outcomes is not known.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract and Discussion state sex-specific results (empathy and prosocial behaviour 'in men'; impaired recognition 'particularly in women') as findings; they are post hoc tests after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (explicit empathy interaction p = 0.092) among at least 42 uncorrected tests. The 60-item AMRS is reported for 8 scales only, out of a number this paper does not state. No means are printed in the text.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors argue that the within-person design gave more power than a parallel design (n above 64); the sex-specific tests rest on 16 people each, and the inequality-aversion test on about 22 (20 degrees of freedom; n not stated).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 32 healthy volunteers, mostly new to MDMA, a single oral dose of 125 mg raised self-ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others and several mood scales against placebo (F(1,31) from 37 to 121 for the three ratings and well-being), raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings for photographs overall (p = 0.019 and 0.047, driven by positive scenes), lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces, and raised plasma oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin. Increases in empathy ratings and in the money-allocation measure were significant in men only by post hoc test; the lowering of accuracy for fearful, angry and sad faces was significant in women only. Hormone changes did not correlate with any emotional or prosocial change. The authors state that most volunteers realised which treatment they had.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say MDMA enhanced emotional empathy and increased prosocial behaviour, altering emotion recognition, empathy and prosociality in a sex-specific way, that these effects likely enhance sociability when MDMA is used recreationally, and that they may be useful in psychotherapy; the Discussion says men showed more empathic concern and less competitive behaviour and that oxytocin is a candidate mediator, while reporting no correlation.

timeline.event: Bedi et al. (Chicago), as cited by these authors: MDMA impaired recognition of fearful faces and did not improve emotion recognition overall, and raised self-rated sociability.
Hysek, Domes and Liechti (same Basel group), as cited: MDMA impaired reading of negative emotions and improved reading of positive emotions in the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test.

Vizeli and Liechti: pooled analysis of nine Basel studies (166 volunteers), whose registrations include both of this study's; positive mood with MDMA across laboratories is reviewed in its Discussion, which also cites this paper for impaired recognition of negative emotions.

replication.where_it_stands: Raised ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others after MDMA are reported by other laboratories as well; the lowered recognition of negative faces was reported earlier by two other studies as cited here. The sex-specific findings and the money-allocation result rest on this study alone and on post hoc subgroup tests.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grants 320030_138481 and 32323B_144996) and the University of Basel (DPH 2053 and DPH 2064) (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: The senior author leads the Basel laboratory whose studies are pooled by Vizeli and Liechti (2017); both registrations cited here appear in that analysis, so the data are probably part of it.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, preregistered study with a check of whether volunteers could tell the capsules apart, equal numbers of women and men sized for the sex-by-drug interaction, outcomes that are behaviours with real consequences, more than one dose, and a setting with other people present, followed by the same measures outside a hospital room.

domains.note: Random order is stated; how the sequence was generated and concealed is not described, and the washout was at least 10 days.
Washout of at least 10 days; the authors say order effects were excluded (no statistics printed).
Identical capsules, but the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had and that this may have biased task performance; no check of the blind.
All 32 are described, but degrees of freedom of 20 and 15 appear without saying who was analysed; no dropout figures.
Self-ratings and tasks by people who knew the condition; the FERT is described as novel; SVO payments were real for two randomly drawn volunteers (amounts not stated).
Registered, but the registered outcomes were not checked; at least 42 tests without correction; the text prints no means; AMRS reported for 8 scales only.

domains.domain: Sex-specific findings (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Post hoc tests of 16 people each after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (0.092 for explicit empathy), uncorrected; the sex-specific results are the paper's headline in the abstract.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison of MDMA with placebo in the same people on the self-rated scales is at some concerns at worst, with very large effects (F 68 to 121) next to the biases named. The overall judgment is set by the sex-specific subgroup findings. The source may be cited for the design and sample, for the rise in self-rated happy, open and close to others and in the listed mood scales, for lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces in all 32 volunteers, and for the unblinding the authors report. It should not be cited as showing that empathy or prosocial behaviour rise in men and not in women, for the size of any effect, or for behaviour outside the laboratory.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 32 healthy volunteers (16 women, 16 men), mean age 25 (SD 3), recruited at the University of Basel; 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; double-blind, random-order crossover, MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) and identical placebo capsules at least 10 days apart; registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Experimental protocol, 1st paragraph; Study drug, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Self-rated effects: MDMA raised visual analogue ratings of feeling happy (F(1,31) = 120.59), open (80.77) and close to others (67.52), all p < 0.001, and AMRS scores for well-being (37.00), extroversion (40.58), emotional excitation (28.46), dreaminess (25.48) and activity (24.48), all p < 0.001, and for inactivity (7.72, p = 0.009) and introversion (10.05, p = 0.003); anxiety was not raised. The text prints no means; they are in Figure 1 and Supplementary Table S1 (not read).

Sex and self-rated happiness: a sex-by-treatment interaction for 'happy' (F(1,31) = 10.49, p = 0.003), but post hoc tests found no difference between men and women after MDMA; no other sex-by-treatment interaction on the self-ratings.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (last two sentences)

key_findings.finding: Empathy test: MDMA raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings across all volunteers (F(1,31) = 6.05, p = 0.019; 4.29, p = 0.047), significant for positive scenes (8.60, p = 0.006; 5.02, p = 0.032) and not for negative scenes; interaction with sex for implicit empathy (4.68, p = 0.039) and a trend for explicit (3.03, p = 0.092); post hoc, the rises were significant in men only (p = 0.025 explicit, 0.022 implicit); cognitive empathy was unchanged.

Money allocation (Social Value Orientation): the prosocial angle rose after MDMA (F(1,31) = 4.42, p = 0.044) with a sex interaction (5.52, p = 0.026); post hoc significant in men (p = 0.008) and not in women; men's level after MDMA equalled women's after placebo; the inequality-aversion index tended to fall (F(1,20) = 3.39, p = 0.079).
key_findings.locator: Results > Social Value Orientation, 1st paragraph; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Face recognition: accuracy fell after MDMA overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, p < 0.001) and for fearful (14.90), angry (18.60), disgusted (5.81, p = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, p = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, p = 0.607); the fall was significant in women (p < 0.001) and not men; in women only, fearful (p < 0.001), angry (p = 0.007) and sad (p = 0.010) faces were named less accurately; the detection threshold for fearful faces rose (F(1,31) = 4.92, printed P < 0.032).
key_findings.locator: Results > Facial emotion recognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Hormones: plasma oxytocin (F(1,31) = 19.84), cortisol (98.70) and prolactin (127.81) rose after MDMA (p < 0.001); copeptin and testosterone did not; no correlation between the hormone changes and the empathy or prosocial changes. Peak MDMA level was higher in women (269.9 ng/mL) than in men (209) at the same 125 mg (1.68 mg/kg in men, 2.09 in women).
key_findings.locator: Results > Endocrine effects and pharmacokinetics of MDMA, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: one dose only, relatively high with obvious subjective effects; although the design was double blind with identical placebo, most volunteers realised which treatment they had, which may have biased task performance; a relatively large number of statistical comparisons; the authors call the dose relevant to recreational and clinical use, citing earlier papers.

The Introduction states, citing earlier laboratory and clinical papers rather than a survey, that enhanced empathy and sociability are also considered a major reason for recreational use of MDMA; this paper presents no data on why people take MDMA.
key_findings.note: Second-hand statement of the authors; the cited papers were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Tests of the treatment-by-sex interaction are printed with 1 and 31 degrees of freedom, though sex is a between-person factor with 32 volunteers, which leaves 30 error degrees of freedom (editors' calculation); the printed p-values fit 30 (for example F 4.68 gives p = 0.0386 with 30 and 0.0383 with 31; printed 0.039), and the fear detection threshold F(1,31) = 4.92 is printed 'P < 0.032' where p = 0.034.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on any conclusion; the models are not described precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of peak plasma MDMA between women and men is printed with 1 and 15 degrees of freedom (F 35.73 and 20.77), and the inequality-aversion test with 1 and 20, without saying how many volunteers were analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Who contributed plasma and inequality-aversion data is unclear; with 32 volunteers a sex comparison would have 30 error degrees of freedom.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion give the sex-specific effects as results (empathy and prosociality 'in men', impaired recognition 'particularly in women'); they rest on post hoc tests after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (p = 0.092 for explicit empathy) among at least 42 uncorrected tests, in 16 people per sex.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the sex differences as hypotheses; the paper's own limitation (a large number of comparisons) applies most to them.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors state that most volunteers realised which treatment they had, yet no check of the blind and no active placebo are reported, and the empathy, money-allocation and face tasks followed the drug effect by 2 to 4 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Task results may partly reflect expectancy; self-ratings of drug effect cannot be blind by nature.

reporting_issues.issue: No means or SDs for any outcome are printed in the text; the results are test statistics and p-values, with values in figures and a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of effects cannot be taken from the article text; the supplement was not read.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4221206, read in the app's browser: abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, figure legends, acknowledgments. Figures 1 to 4 are images and were not read for values; Supplementary Table S1 and Figures S1 to S3 are separate files and were not read.
